title: What to Check Before You Trust a Browser Extension
content:
A browser extension that saves one click may also request access to every website you open. Before installing it, decide whether its job justifies that access, whether you can identify who operates it, and how you will remove it. These checks help you make a defensible decision; they cannot certify that software is harmless.

Start with the job and the publisher

Write one sentence describing the task: save selected research links, block unwanted page elements, or translate a paragraph. Check whether the browser already offers an adequate feature. An extension you do not install needs no ongoing permission review.

Find the listing in the browser's official extension store. Compare the publisher name, linked website, support contact, and privacy policy. Follow the developer's own website back to the listing where possible. Similar names and logos are weak identity evidence. Treat an unexplained mismatch as a reason to pause.

Read recent reviews for specific complaints about changed behavior, unexpected redirects, or missing exports. Reviews can point you toward questions; download counts, stars, and a polished listing do not answer them. A public source repository can help a knowledgeable reviewer inspect code, but its existence alone does not establish what the installed package contains.

Translate permissions into consequences

Read the permission prompt before approving it. Mozilla explains that access to data on all websites can include page content and information entered into pages, including usernames and passwords. That capability can serve legitimate tools, including password managers and blockers, so broad access requires an explanation rather than an automatic verdict. See Mozilla's permission explanations.

  • For page access, ask which sites require it and whether access can start only when you invoke the tool.
  • For history, clipboard, or download permissions, identify the feature that needs each capability.
  • For a separate application or proxy setting, ask why the browser feature depends on it.
  • For optional features, decline permissions you do not need and check whether the core task still works.

Permissions describe potential access, not a complete record of collection. Read the privacy policy separately: what leaves the device, which service receives it, how long it remains, and how to request deletion. If a summarizer sends selected text to a server, that should be understandable before you provide confidential material. Vague assurances about respecting privacy do not resolve an unexplained data flow.

Reduce access before using real accounts

Chrome

Open chrome://extensions, choose the extension's Details, and inspect site access. Where available, choose access when selected or restrict it to specific sites. Leave incognito and local-file access off unless necessary. Google's extension management instructions explain these controls and an important limit: site-access changes do not constrain lower-level VPN or proxy capabilities.

Firefox

Open about:addons, select Extensions, and open the extension's permissions panel. Turn off unnecessary optional permissions. Mozilla documents these switches in its optional-permissions guide. Available controls depend on the extension; do not assume every required permission can be revoked while keeping it enabled. If the access you need to restrict is mandatory, choose another tool or remove it.

Test with less to expose

Use a separate test profile without personal sign-ins, synced passwords, or confidential tabs. Chrome profiles separate browsing information, but this is not a security sandbox or an audit of the extension's network traffic. Keep browser sync off during the trial. Anything you enter into the test profile may still be exposed to the extension's granted capabilities. A quiet trial cannot prove future safety.

Hypothetical example: a research clipper

This is a hypothetical decision, not a product test. Maya wants to save selected paragraphs from public gardening articles. A clipper requests access to every website and asks her to create a cloud account. Its policy says saved text is uploaded, but does not explain retention.

Maya first checks whether bookmarks meet her need. If she still needs clipping, she asks whether the extension can work only when selected and whether local export is available. She declines unrelated optional permissions and tries a public paragraph containing no personal information.

A successful clip would demonstrate that the feature works under those conditions. It would not prove that the extension sends nothing else, will behave identically after an update, or is suitable for her employer's documents. If retention remains unclear, she keeps confidential material out and chooses a different workflow.

Keep updates, but reconsider new access

Do not freeze an extension indefinitely to preserve familiar behavior. Mozilla recommends automatic add-on updates and warns that disabling them can mean missing security fixes. In Firefox's Extensions panel, use the gear menu to check updates and update settings; see Mozilla's update instructions.

Chrome can disable an extension when an update adds a permission that triggers a warning, until you accept that permission. Google's permission warning guidelines explain this behavior. Read the new request against your original task before re-enabling. An update without a warning is not a fresh guarantee: changed behavior may fit existing permissions.

Revisit the publisher, policy, and permissions when ownership, purpose, or your own usage changes. If you stop using a feature, reconsider the required permissions it justified: leaving the feature idle does not itself revoke access. Restrict what the browser allows, then remove or replace the extension if retained access exceeds your remaining need. Ask your administrator about mandatory work extensions.

Keep an exit copy

Before storing valuable notes in an extension, export a sample and confirm that another application can read it. Check whether the export includes attachments and annotations you need. Keep important material outside the extension as well. Export supports continuity if the tool disappears; it cannot recover confidentiality once information has been uploaded or disclosed.

Remove first when behavior breaks trust

For unexpected redirects or unexplained access requests, stop using the extension. In Chrome, open Manage extensions and select Remove. In Firefox, open Extensions and themes, find the extension, and use its menu to remove it; Mozilla documents disabling and removal. Note its name, version, and suspicious behavior for support.

Uninstalling does not by itself delete a provider account, erase uploaded data, or revoke a separate account connection. Open each connected service's security or connected-apps settings and revoke access you no longer want. Request deletion through the provider's documented process; revoking access stops authorization, not necessarily retention. If credentials may have been exposed, change affected passwords and end active sessions from a trusted device.

Decision checklist

  • Can I identify the publisher and explain why I need this extension?
  • Does every retained permission serve a feature I still use?
  • Have I restricted sites and understood what leaves the browser?
  • Can I export my work, remove the extension, and revoke linked accounts?

Install only when these answers are clear. Defer when the publisher's explanation is incomplete; remove when the access no longer fits the job.
excerpt: Check extension publishers, permissions, site access, and privacy, then review updates, test with less exposure, and remove unwanted account connections.

title: What to Keep in a Personal Backup Plan
content:
A personal backup plan should let you recover a missing photograph, finish tomorrow's work, and regain access to your accounts after losing your main device. Keep the files, the keys needed to unlock them, and a short set of recovery instructions. A drive full of unidentified folders is only part of that plan.

Start with one question: if your laptop and phone disappeared tonight, what would you need first? Use the answer to choose what to copy, how often to copy it, and where to keep a separate copy.

Keep an inventory of irreplaceable files

Write down actual folders and services rather than broad labels such as “everything important.” Check Downloads, external drives, phone storage, and application libraries as well as Documents. Separate material you created from material you can download again.

  • Personal records: identification scans, household documents, receipts, and records you need to retain. Store sensitive copies with encryption and limit access.
  • Original work: drafts, spreadsheets, source files, research notes, and project assets. Include the editable originals, not only exported PDFs.
  • Memories: original photographs, videos, recordings, and any captions or catalog information that make them understandable.
  • Service exports: important contacts, calendars, notes, and messages where the service provides an export. Record the format and how to open it.
  • Rebuild information: application names, legitimate download locations, license details, bookmarks, and a short list of essential browser extensions.

Record exclusions too. Replaceable installers and temporary files may not deserve space, but an excluded project folder might. For cloud files, confirm that the backup contains downloadable content rather than placeholders. Open a sample while disconnected from the internet.

Keep exports usable outside the original account

Where available, keep an open or widely supported export alongside the native file: plain text for notes, CSV for simple tables, or original image files. Check the trade-offs: CSV may lose formulas and formatting; PDF may preserve appearance without editability. Keep native sources and linked assets when needed, and open a sample without signing into the original service.

Keep copies with different failure paths

A practical starting arrangement is your working files, a versioned local backup, and a separate off-site copy. The off-site copy protects against losing everything in one room; version history helps when you notice an overwrite later. Choose the arrangement around the failures you need to survive.

Synchronization makes files available across devices, but deletions and unwanted edits may also spread. Check the service's deleted-file recovery, version retention, storage limits, and account-recovery requirements before treating it as your recovery copy.

Include an offline copy that is disconnected after backup completes. CISA's ransomware guidance recommends offline, encrypted backups and regular recovery testing because ransomware can attack accessible backups. A permanently attached USB disk does not provide that separation.

Write down how much recent work you can afford to lose. If redoing one day's writing is acceptable, schedule around that requirement; if a single recording is irreplaceable, copy it after capture. Also decide how far back you need versions. A successful backup today cannot recover an older version already removed by retention rules.

Keep recovery access separate from the device

Encryption protects a lost backup disk, but you must still be able to unlock it. Record where the backup password or recovery key is held without putting the secret in a public checklist. Avoid making your lost phone the only route to your password manager, backup account, and second authentication factor.

Keep account recovery codes in a protected location you can reach independently, such as secured paper storage. Treat them as credentials. Avoid loose plaintext password exports; if an export is necessary, protect it immediately and remove temporary unprotected copies.

Check backup encryption itself rather than assuming laptop encryption covers an external copy. Apple's Time Machine security instructions distinguish local and network backup encryption changes; changing some network backups to encrypted storage erases the existing backup set. Read the applicable instructions before converting your only copy.

Keep a restore procedure you can follow

Windows: verify coverage and the destination

Microsoft's File History instructions explain backing up personal files to an external drive or network location, adding folders through libraries, and restoring previous versions. Inspect your actual folder coverage. Use Restore to when you need a different destination; replacing a current version can overwrite work you intended to keep.

Mac: check the version before restoring

Apple's Time Machine restore guide explains browsing earlier backups and restoring selected items to their original locations. For a rehearsal, use a disposable document with recognizable contents and preserve any current copy before restoring. A successful document recovery does not prove that every application or a complete replacement Mac will recover correctly.

Keep a manifest beside the backup

A manifest connects each important item to a recovery route. Keep a readable copy with the backup and another reachable without your main device. Include credential locations, not secrets.

  • Item: name the folder, device, or service, including locations outside default backup folders.
  • Priority: identify what you need first and what can wait.
  • Destinations: identify local, off-site, and disconnected copies by recognizable names.
  • Schedule: record the intended backup interval and version-retention period.
  • Dependencies: name the export format, required application, and linked assets.
  • Evidence: record the last completed backup, latest restore check, and unresolved gaps.

For browser rebuilding, keep exported bookmarks, essential extension names, and supported settings exports as part of the application inventory. Rebuild what you need; avoid relying solely on an old browser profile.

A hypothetical plan for one laptop and phone

Hypothetical example: Maya writes freelance reports and keeps family photographs. She chooses daily versioned backups for active reports, copies new photo originals after importing them, and maintains an encrypted off-site copy. Once a week she connects an encrypted external drive, completes a backup, ejects it, and stores it separately. Her offline copy can therefore lag behind her daily copy.

Her recovery note identifies the folders, backup destinations, credential location, and restore order: account access, active reports, then photographs. Each month she restores a sample report and photo and records whether they open. These are illustrative choices, not tested results or a universal schedule.

A hypothetical restore-log entry

This template uses an invented filename and proposed checks, not completed test results. Leave the result pending until you perform the rehearsal.

Item: Projects/Client-A/report.docx
Source: encrypted external drive, earlier version
Destination: separate rehearsal folder
Checks: opens; expected text present; linked images available
Result: pending rehearsal
Follow-up: record missing assets or access problems

Record failures precisely. An unavailable password needs an independent access route; missing images need broader coverage. Repeating an incomplete backup fixes neither problem.

Check the plan before you need it

  • Confirm the last successful backup and investigate skipped files or storage warnings.
  • Restore an older version as well as a recent file; inspect content, not just filenames.
  • Check that credentials remain reachable without your main device.
  • Review new folders, devices, accounts, and changed retention settings.
  • Record what remains unprotected and the next action needed to cover it.

If malware is suspected, use a clean recovery environment before reconnecting backup media. A backup cannot undo stolen information or guarantee clean software. Keep the plan useful by stating exactly what you can recover, from which copy, and what your latest restore check actually demonstrated.
excerpt: Build a personal backup plan around irreplaceable files, encrypted copies, independent recovery access, and restore checks you can repeat.
